read: partial: pp.1-11 (abstract, introduction, benchmark statistics and task structure, evaluation pipeline, construction, experiments, iterative design, failure analysis, related work, conclusion) in full; appendices A (limitations, p.26), B (opening, pp.26-27), C.1-C.2 (p.28) and D.1-D.3 (pp.28-30) read; task examples (appendix E onward) and the NeurIPS checklist skimmed or searched
venue_now: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p.1 footer); arXiv 2509.16204v2, 6 Nov 2025 (p.1)
what_it_is: EngDesign is a benchmark of 101 open-ended engineering design tasks in nine domains (operating systems, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structures, digital hardware, analog IC, robotics, signal processing), decomposed into 473 gradable rubric items (p.3; Table 1, p.5). Each task has a task description, a per-task rubric scored out of 100 with partial credit, an automated evaluation pipeline and a validated reference design (p.5). The model answers in a structured format with a step-by-step reasoning field and a ConfigFile holding the design; the pipeline reads the design fields and runs domain-specific simulation (e.g. SPICE, finite element analysis, MATLAB Control System Toolbox) to return pass/fail, a 0-100 score and a log (pp.2, 4-6, 30). Tasks were proposed by graduate students and researchers, pre-tested with o4-mini and reviewed in two rounds, the second by faculty domain experts (p.6); 101 of 186 proposals were kept (p.28). Twelve LLMs were evaluated with three trials per task; the best overall pass rate is 34.38% (o3) and every model scores 0% on analog IC design (p.7).
domain: engineering design: operating systems, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structural design, digital hardware, analog integrated circuits, robotics, signal processing (p.2; Table 1, p.5)
size: 101 tasks, 473 rubric items, 9 domains; 67 open tasks (EngDesign-Open) and 34 that need licensed software such as MATLAB or Cadence; 23 tasks include images (pp.3, 5); 12 LLMs evaluated (p.7)
source_of_items: expert-written: proposed by graduate students and researchers from open-source resources and their own domain knowledge, then reviewed in two rounds (p.6)
has_gold_traces: no: each task has a validated reference design that meets all requirements (p.5), not a reasoning trace; there are no gold intermediate steps
evaluation: simulation-based functional verification of the final design, with per-task rubric partial credit (0-100) and a pass/fail flag (pp.5-6); the pipeline reads only the design fields of the structured answer, and the paper describes no scoring of the step-by-step reasoning field it requests (pp.4, 6, 30); a manual failure analysis labels error types in three models' failed responses (p.9)
human_validation: Two review rounds: the first checks task clarity, the rubric, that the evaluation code runs and that the reference design passes; the second is by faculty domain experts (p.6). 101 of 186 proposals from over 40 contributors were accepted and 85 discarded (p.28). No comparison of the pipeline's scores with expert judgements is reported. The failure analysis was annotated by hand, multi-label, for o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p.9).
contamination_measures: none reported; the tasks are newly written by contributors (p.6) and the dataset is public (p.1)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' Also covered by the closing generalisation S-E3 (L199-205): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-E2: 'design generation' is right; EngDesign asks models to produce functional designs such as controllers, analog circuits and structures (pp.1-2). Calling design a 'tangential skill' is loose: the paper presents design as the core of engineering practice (p.2), and its tasks demand the quantitative, constraint-driven physical reasoning EngTrace targets, e.g. choosing a steel beam's thickness from its loads and material properties (Fig. 1, p.3) or meeting gain- and phase-margin requirements (p.4). The sentence also never names EngDesign, so a reader cannot tell which benchmark is meant. S-E3: it is true that only the outcome is assessed, since the pipeline reads only the design (pp.4, 6, 30), but 'outcome matching' does not fit: designs are non-unique, so there is no golden answer to match, and the design is checked by simulation with partial credit (p.5). Overall imprecise; the S-E3 part borders on misleading, because the paper's main claim is a move away from 'static answer checking' to simulation-driven verification (p.1).

suggested_wording: EngDesign (Guo et al., 2025b) asks models for designs in nine engineering domains, from controllers and analog circuits to structures, and checks the final design by domain-specific simulation against the task's requirements with rubric-based partial credit, without scoring the reasoning that produced it.
facts_to_cite: 101 design tasks in nine engineering domains, with 473 gradable rubric items (p.3; Table 1, p.5)
Each task has a task description, a rubric scored out of 100 with partial credit, an automated evaluation pipeline and a validated reference design (p.5)

The design is parsed from a structured response and checked by domain-specific simulation (e.g. SPICE, finite element analysis, MATLAB Control System Toolbox), giving pass/fail, a 0-100 score and an evaluation log (pp.2, 5-6)
Models are asked for a step-by-step reasoning field as well, but the evaluation pipeline reads the design fields (pp.4, 6, 30)
Tasks were proposed by graduate students and researchers, pre-tested with o4-mini and reviewed in two rounds, the second by faculty domain experts (p.6); 101 of 186 proposals were accepted (p.28)
34 tasks need licensed software (MATLAB, Cadence); the other 67 form EngDesign-Open (pp.3, 5)
Twelve LLMs, three trials per task: no model passes more than 35% of tasks (best, o3, 34.38%), and every model scores 0% on analog IC design (p.7)
With evaluation feedback over ten iterations, o3 reaches almost a 60% pass rate on a 71-task subset (p.9 and footnote 2)
In a manual failure analysis of three models, domain-knowledge errors and constraint violations account for roughly 55-67% of failures, and pure computation errors for at most 9% (pp.9-10)
Published at NeurIPS 2025, Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p.1)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: an engineering domain across several branches (its control, structures, mechanical-systems and signal-processing tasks overlap EngTrace's branches); expert-reviewed tasks with a reference solution; a physics-grounded, non-LLM checker (simulation) rather than an LLM judge. Lacks: generated instances (101 hand-written, static tasks); gold reasoning traces (only a reference design); step-level or process evaluation (only the final design is scored; the reasoning field is not); expert validation of the evaluator (the evaluation code is reviewed, but no agreement between pipeline scores and experts is reported); any contamination measure. The task type also differs: open-ended design with non-unique solutions, against EngTrace's analysis problems with computed reference answers.
notes: The May reference entry gives only the arXiv id; the paper appeared at NeurIPS 2025 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track), so the entry should be updated. The May text never names the benchmark (EngDesign). An error in the paper: Table 5 (p.30) gives the model pointer for 'Gemini-2.0-Flash' as 'gemini-1.5-pro'. The verdict turns on the word 'tangential' and on S-E3's 'outcome matching'; the description 'design generation' itself is right.
